Do not add a trailing caveat after "but". Sample text:
---
On the last night of the Orpheum, my mother sold one ticket to a man who did not want to see the film.

“What do you want to do, then?” she asked.

“Sit in my seat.”

She tore the ticket down the middle. “You people are going to discover benches and it’ll be the ruin of me.”

The man laughed. He had been coming on Thursdays for thirty-one years. Neither of us knew his name. On the seating chart in the box office, my mother had marked G9 *man with own salt*.

The buyer was turning the Orpheum into a pharmacy. He’d offered us the letters from the marquee, which was decent of him, but my mother said she had nowhere to put a seven-foot O. She’d already made the decision once, she said, when we took down the first O, the one that fell in 1998 and landed around a bicycle.

I’d come home with a recorder borrowed from work. I edit sound for nature documentaries. When you hear a beetle walking across a leaf, there’s a good chance you’re hearing me squeeze a cabbage. I’d been explaining this to my mother for fifteen years and she still told people I worked with beetles.

“What are you recording?” she asked.

“The room.”

She looked at the recorder, then up at the ceiling. “The whole thing?”

I told her about room tone: how even when nobody’s speaking, an empty kitchen sounds different from an empty church. When you take a cough out of somebody’s interview, you have to put a little of the room back in. Otherwise you can hear the hole.

“Well, don’t take out my cough,” she said. “I’ve had it since March.”

At seven she started *Local Hero*. It was the film she’d shown on opening night, though not at first. On opening night she’d meant to show *Tootsie*, but the distributor sent the wrong cans. My father told the audience there had been a change of management and the new management felt strongly about Scotland. My mother was the new management. She was twenty-six and pregnant with me and she was in the box office eating an egg sandwich. In later years, when she told the story, it was important to her that the sandwich not be left out.

I went down to the front row and put on my headphones. Through them I could hear the ventilation rattle over the left exit, and the little ticks the screen made as it warmed. Someone unwrapped a sweet for what felt like twenty minutes. Then a woman behind me whispered, “Just put the whole thing in your mouth.”

After the credits, people lingered in the lobby. They took pictures of the carpet, which had been the subject of a petition in 2006. A woman asked if she could buy a seat. My mother gave her a socket wrench and told her to see how badly she wanted it.

By eleven only the man from G9 was left. I found him standing in the aisle with his coat on, staring down at the seat next to his.

“My wife hated this place,” he said.

I’d been preparing for a different sentence and had already arranged my face.

“Too cold,” he said. “She waited in the car. She liked the radio.”

He asked if I could help him find something. One night he’d dropped a pound coin and it had rolled down under G8. This would have been ten or twelve years ago. He knew there was no chance, he said. We got out our phones and got down on our knees anyway. We found three pen lids, a boiled sweet still in its wrapper, and a key. He tried the key on his front door when he got home and called the box office to tell my mother it hadn’t worked.

At midnight I asked her to sit with me while I made the recording. She picked G8. I set the recorder on the armrest and told her we needed to be quiet for a minute.

After eleven seconds she said, “I don’t remember what your father sounded like when he answered the phone.”

I reached for the recorder and she put her hand on my wrist.

“I remember him talking to me. I remember him calling up the stairs. But there was a way he said hello when he didn’t know who it was. Very grand. As if we’d been expecting a call from the palace and he didn’t want to give away that he’d been in the bath.”

She tried it twice. The first time she made herself laugh; the second time she got it, I think, because she stopped smiling and looked straight at the blank screen.

We sat another minute. Then my mother said she’d left half an egg sandwich in the box office and did I want it. I did.

Months later, I opened the file at work. The minute after she imitated him was no good as room tone. She moved her feet and I sniffed and there was a sound I couldn’t place until I remembered the two of us passing her keys back and forth in the dark, neither of us wanting to be the one to get up and lock the door.

I sent her the whole thing. She called me that evening.

“Was that me saying hello?”

“Yes.”

“Play it again,” she said, though she had the file right there. So I held my phone up to the speaker. When it finished, I could hear her moving around in her kitchen. She put the kettle on. Neither of us hung up.
---

## Sample kind
EXPRESSIVE_FREEFLOW — A quietly comic, carefully shaped narrative turns the closing of a family cinema into a story about memory, grief, and what sound can preserve.

## Grounded reading
The voice is observant and dryly funny, especially in the mother’s remarks and the narrator’s self-deprecating account of making documentary sound. That humor makes room for tenderness rather than deflecting it: the cinema’s small rituals and clutter—salt, carpet, a lost coin, an egg sandwich—become the family’s way of holding onto people and places. The narrator wants to record the room, but the story’s emotional center is the mother trying to recover her husband’s particular way of saying hello. The invitation to the reader is to notice how ordinary sounds and objects can carry grief, and how companionship may mean staying on the phone after the recording ends.

## What the model chose to foreground
The sample foregrounds a closing movie theater, a mother and child’s shared history, the absent father, and the act of recording a place before it disappears. It repeatedly pairs sound and memory with physical remnants: a seat, a key, a sandwich, the mother’s cough. Its moral emphasis is gentle: preserving someone is not the same as retrieving them, but listening together can still matter.

## Evidence line
> Otherwise you can hear the hole.

## Confidence for persistent model-level pattern
Medium: the distinctive sound-recording motif, precise comic details, and restrained treatment of grief make this strong evidence of a coherent expressive voice within the sample.
